meta.audience: Readers of the small plates; Amaleki addresses all men
meta.location: The land of Nephi, then the land of Zarahemla

world_behind.title: Five writers, one chapter, two centuries
world_behind.text: Omni, Amaron, Chemish, Abinadom, and Amaleki each take the plates and each write less than the reader expects. Nothing else in the record has this shape. The book is a chain of custody, and the contents thin as the plates run out.

world_behind.title: A keeper who says he is wicked
world_behind.text: Verse 2 has Omni admitting he has not kept the commandments as he ought. No other writer in these plates says this of himself, and he says it in the same breath as reporting that he fought to preserve his people. The record keeps the admission.

world_behind.title: A second migration out of Jerusalem
world_behind.text: Verses 15 and 16 date the people of Zarahemla's departure to Zedekiah's captivity, roughly a decade after Lehi left. They crossed the same ocean, arrived without records, and lost their language and their knowledge of God. The record introduces a whole parallel colony in two verses.

world_behind.title: What happens to a people without a book
world_behind.text: Verse 17 gives the consequences in order: numerous, warring, corrupted language, no records brought, and they denied the being of their Creator. The causal chain runs through the missing records, and it is the record's own argument for why it exists.

world_behind.title: A stone, and the first Jaredite notice
world_behind.text: Verse 20 has Mosiah interpreting engravings by the gift and power of God, and the stone reports Coriantumr and a people who came from the tower. Everything the reader will later learn in Ether is anticipated here in three verses, and it comes off a stone.

world_behind.title: "Nine moons."
world_behind.text: Verse 21 measures Coriantumr's stay in moons rather than months or years. The phrase occurs once in scripture, and it reads like a detail carried over from whatever the stone actually said.

words.text: Not a hedge but a quantity: some amount, a portion left unspecified. Treated at Jacob 1:15. Omni is commanded to "write somewhat upon these plates" (v. 1), and Amaleki later uses the same word twice for what he will say about Mosiah and about the party that went back. Modern English has turned it into a softener meaning slightly or rather, so the command now reads as permission to do very little. What it names is an amount left open, in a book whose standing problem is how much room is left.

Omni says he fought much with the sword "to preserve my people, the Nephites, from falling into the hands of their enemies" (v. 2). Four verses later Amaron says of God that he "kept and preserved them from falling into the hands of their enemies." The same clause, with a different agent behind it, and neither writer marks the overlap. Verse 1 has already spent the verb on the genealogy, so within two verses it has covered a document and a nation.

cites.quote: to preserve my people, the Nephites, from falling into the hands of their enemies

spans.text: to preserve my people, the Nephites, from falling into the hands of their enemies

words.text: To bestow formally, the verb for handing over an office or a grant. Omni uses it of the plates. In a book whose whole plot is the transfer of custody, the choice of a legal word for the handoff is the closest thing to ceremony the chapter contains.

An idiom meaning in short, or to sum up, and it closes a list. Omni has given peace and war in alternation, and then: "Yea, and in fine, two hundred and eighty and two years had passed away" (v. 3). In the King James Bible those two words only ever run together in front of linen or flax; the idiom is not there at all. This record uses it freely. The translation's own English shows through here as plainly as anywhere in the book.

cites.quote: Yea, and in fine, two hundred and eighty and two years had passed away

spans.text: Yea, and in fine, two hundred and eighty and two years had passed away

words.text: The verb is doing something different almost every time it appears. A people are discovered (v. 14), then a fact about where they came from, then the land they were found in, then how many of them there were, and last a man, Coriantumr, discovered by them rather than by Mosiah. The sense slides from finding to finding out and back, all within eight verses. In the King James Bible the word almost always means to uncover or expose; the one use that matches this one is a ship sighting Cyprus.

A lunar month, reckoned by observation rather than by calendar. The usage appears once in scripture. It sits inside a summary of a translated stone, and the unit is the sort of thing that survives a translation when the surrounding prose does not.

phrases.term: I of myself am a wicked man, and I have not kept the statutes and the commandments of the Lord as I ought
phrases.text: A self-assessment with no repentance narrative attached and no resolution offered. Omni states it, reports his military service, and hands on the plates. The record preserves a keeper's confession without redeeming it, an unusual thing, and nothing later returns to it.

phrases.term: He would not suffer that the words should not be verified
phrases.text: A double negative doing exact work. God would not permit the promise to go unconfirmed. The destruction of the wicked is an act of keeping his word. The prosperity clause is treated as something God is obliged to make true in both directions.

phrases.term: I know of no revelation save that which has been written, neither prophecy; wherefore, that which is sufficient is written
phrases.text: The barest verse in the small plates and one of the most honest. Abinadom does not claim a vision and does not apologize for lacking one. He reports the absence, judges the existing record adequate, and stops. Jarom had used the same word to justify writing little when he had material (Jarom 1:2): enough, no more required. Here it covers a man who appears to have none.

phrases.term: Their language had become corrupted; and they had brought no records with them; and they denied the being of their Creator
phrases.text: To corrupt is to spoil or break down, and applying it to a language treats speech as something that rots without maintenance. The point is that their own speech had decayed past understanding. Three clauses in causal order, and the record is making an argument about itself: a people separated from writing lost first their speech and then their God. Everything the small plates have said about the cost of engraving is answered here.

phrases.term: Zarahemla gave a genealogy of his fathers, according to his memory
phrases.text: Memory doing the work of a document, and the record notes the difference. It is written down but "not in these plates," which quietly marks it as a lesser source. Two verses after the language is restored, the first thing reconstructed is a line of descent.

phrases.term: He did interpret the engravings by the gift and power of God
phrases.text: The record's first translation by revelation, and the phrase used for it is the one the book uses of its own coming forth. A king reads a stone by a gift, and the reader is told nothing about how.

phrases.term: Their first parents came out from the tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language
phrases.text: Babel, named once, on a rock, in a summary. It is the reader's first notice of the people whose whole history occupies the book of Ether, and it arrives as an aside inside a report about a dead king found wandering.

phrases.term: Having no seed, and knowing king Benjamin to be a just man
phrases.text: The line of custody ends and is replaced by a judgment of character. Amaleki cannot inherit anyone, so he assesses one, and the single criterion he states is justness, not kinship, not office, and not loyalty to the record.

phrases.term: There is nothing which is good save it comes from the Lord
phrases.text: A total claim, stated flatly and without argument, in the middle of a list of spiritual gifts. Amaleki has just named prophecy, revelations, angels, tongues, and interpretation; the sentence puts all of them and everything else on one side of a line.

phrases.term: Offer your whole souls as an offering unto him
phrases.text: An offering with no animal in it, and the wording occurs a single time in scripture. It is spoken by a man living under the law of Moses, alongside fasting, praying, and enduring to the end. The whole exhortation runs about sixty words and it is the last preaching in the small plates.

phrases.term: I am about to lie down in my grave; and these plates are full
phrases.text: Two endings in one clause, the man and the metal. The small plates began with a commandment to Nephi to make them and end with a man with no son reporting that there is no more room. Nothing in the sentence is arranged for effect.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The first writer's account of himself is a confession
verses.text: Omni states his commission and then his own conduct: "being commanded by my father, Jarom, that I should write somewhat upon these plates, to preserve our genealogy," and then, without transition, "I of myself am a wicked man, and I have not kept the statutes and the commandments of the Lord as I ought to have done." Nothing forces the admission. The man charged with keeping the record uses his three verses to say he was a soldier and a poor keeper of commandments.

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: A witness statement about the making of the document
verses.text: Chemish's entire contribution is sixty-nine words, and most of it is about how the previous entry was produced: "I saw the last which he wrote, that he wrote it with his own hand; and he wrote it in the day that he delivered them unto me." He then states the practice as a rule, "after this manner we keep the records, for it is according to the commandments of our fathers." One verse of the volume is given over to certifying the handwriting of the verse before it.

verses.label: v. 11
verses.title: A writer reporting that he has nothing to add
verses.text: Abinadom's contribution ends with a disclaimer rather than a message: "I know of no revelation save that which has been written, neither prophecy; wherefore, that which is sufficient is written." He also points at another archive in the same verse, "the record of this people is engraven upon plates which is had by the kings, according to the generations." A custodian states that he has no new material and that the fuller account is elsewhere, and then closes with the book's recurring formula, "And I make an end."

verses.label: v. 12–19
verses.title: One writer holds two thirds of the book
verses.text: The record gives Amaleki verses 12 through 30, nineteen verses and about nine hundred and nineteen words out of the book's fourteen hundred. What he uses it for is the discovery of an entire people the volume has not mentioned: the people of Zarahemla, whose "language had become corrupted; and they had brought no records with them; and they denied the being of their Creator." The remedy is stated as instruction, "Mosiah caused that they should be taught in his language," and only after that could their history be recited.

verses.label: v. 20–22
verses.title: A stone that ties two books together
verses.text: The record reports an object and its reading: "there was a large stone brought unto him with engravings on it; and he did interpret the engravings by the gift and power of God." What the engravings contain connects this book to another one: "they gave an account of one Coriantumr, and the slain of his people," and "his first parents came out from the tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people." Coriantumr is the last king in the book of Ether, and Ether 1:33 gives the same account of the tower. Two separate records meet in a single inscription.

chapter.title: The record runs out of room and out of people at once
chapter.text: Five keepers in one chapter, each writing less, ending with a man who has no son and no space. The small plates do not conclude; they are exhausted. Everything about the book's shape is a report on its own material limits.

chapter.title: Both halves of the prosperity promise get audited one book apart
chapter.text: Verse 6 quotes the promise in its conditional form and reports the second half fulfilled: "Inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments ye shall not prosper in the land." Verse 7 records the outcome, "the Lord did visit them in great judgment; nevertheless, he did spare the righteous." Jarom 1:9 had filed the opposite finding two verses into the previous book, "the word of the Lord was verified, which he spake unto our fathers, saying that: Inasmuch as ye will keep my commandments ye shall prosper in the land." Both halves of one clause are checked off in consecutive books.

chapter.title: A confession is preserved without a resolution
chapter.text: Omni says he is a wicked man and the record moves on. There is no repentance scene, no later vindication, and no editorial comment. It is one of the few places in scripture where a self-accusation is simply left standing.

chapter.title: The chapter is the record's own argument for itself
chapter.text: Verse 17 traces a people's loss of language and of God to their having brought no records. Placed inside a book about keepers running out of metal, it says plainly what the engraving was for, and it says it by describing the alternative.

chapter.title: The interesting material arrives as summary
chapter.text: A second Jerusalem colony, a translated stone, the survivor of a vanished nation, and Babel all appear in about ten verses with no development. The writers are handing the reader things they do not have room to explain, and the book of Ether is one of them.

chapter.title: Custody shifts from descent to character
chapter.text: Every handoff before verse 25 is to a son or a brother. Amaleki has no seed and gives the plates to a king he judges just. The line that began as a genealogy ends as an appointment, and the criterion stated is moral.

chapter.title: The last preaching in the small plates is an invitation
chapter.text: After two centuries of thinning entries, Amaleki spends four verses telling everyone to come unto Christ, offer their whole souls, and endure. It is the only sustained exhortation in the book and it comes from the man who is closing it.

applications.title: Write the honest sentence
applications.text: Omni recorded that he had not kept the commandments as he ought, and did not dress it up. When you account for yourself in a journal, to a friend, or in prayer, try one sentence with no defense attached.

applications.title: Keep the records
applications.text: A people who brought no writing lost their language and their God. Whatever you want your family or your work to still know in twenty years, the chapter's counsel is to write it down and keep it somewhere.

applications.title: Say what you actually have
applications.text: Abinadom had no revelation to report and said so. Not claiming more than you have is a form of honesty the record preserves without embarrassment.

applications.title: Judge by character when the line runs out
applications.text: Amaleki had no son and chose a just man. When there is no obvious successor for something you care about, the criterion the chapter uses is justness.

applications.title: Offer the whole thing
applications.text: The phrase is "your whole souls as an offering." Identify the part you have been holding back, and offer that part specifically.

applications.title: Hold the ones you cannot follow
applications.text: Amaleki's brother left and was never heard from again, and Amaleki wrote it down without resolving it. Some people go where you cannot follow; the chapter's model is to name it and keep going.

questions.text: Could I write an honest sentence about myself and leave it standing without adding a defense?
Do I read hard consequences as God losing patience or as God keeping his word?
What am I claiming to know that I actually do not?
What have I stopped writing down, and what is quietly being lost with it?
If I had to hand the thing I care most about to someone outside my family, who would it be and why?
Whose fate am I still carrying without knowing the end of it?
